claim: Low voltage-activated calcium currents are mediated by T-type calcium channels CaV3.1, CaV3.2, and CaV3.3.
source: Low voltage-activated calcium currents are mediated by T-type calcium channels CaV3.1, CaV3.2, and CaV3.3, which modulate a variety of physiological processes including sleep, cardiac pace-making, pain, and epilepsy.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about T-type calcium channels and their role in mediating low voltage-activated calcium currents.

claim: T-type calcium channels modulate a variety of physiological processes including sleep, cardiac pace-making, pain, and epilepsy.
source: Low voltage-activated calcium currents are mediated by T-type calcium channels CaV3.1, CaV3.2, and CaV3.3, which modulate a variety of physiological processes including sleep, cardiac pace-making, pain, and epilepsy.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific knowledge about the physiological roles of T-type calcium channels.

claim: CaV3 isoforms' biophysical properties, overlapping expression, and lack of subtype-selective pharmacology hinder the determination of their specific physiological roles in health and disease.
source: CaV3 isoforms' biophysical properties, overlapping expression, and lack of subtype-selective pharmacology hinder the determination of their specific physiological roles in health and disease.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges in studying CaV3 isoforms, supported by inference from the state of the field.

claim: μ-theraphotoxin Pn3a is the first subtype-selective spider venom peptide inhibitor of CaV3.3.
source: We have identified μ-theraphotoxin Pn3a as the first subtype-selective spider venom peptide inhibitor of CaV3.3, with >100-fold lower potency against the other T-type isoforms.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing selective inhibition of CaV3.3.

claim: Pn3a has >100-fold lower potency against CaV3.1 and CaV3.2 compared to CaV3.3.
source: We have identified μ-theraphotoxin Pn3a as the first subtype-selective spider venom peptide inhibitor of CaV3.3, with >100-fold lower potency against the other T-type isoforms.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing differential inhibition across CaV3 isoforms.

claim: Pn3a modifies CaV3.3 gating through a depolarizing shift in the voltage dependence of activation.
source: Pn3a modifies CaV3.3 gating through a depolarizing shift in the voltage dependence of activation thus decreasing CaV3.3-mediated currents in the normal range of activation potentials.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing changes in voltage-dependent activation.

claim: Pn3a decreases CaV3.3-mediated currents in the normal range of activation potentials.
source: Pn3a modifies CaV3.3 gating through a depolarizing shift in the voltage dependence of activation thus decreasing CaV3.3-mediated currents in the normal range of activation potentials.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing current inhibition.

claim: Pn3a preferentially binds to the S3-S4 region of domain II (CaV3.3DII).
source: Paddle chimeras of KV1.7 channels bearing voltage sensor sequences from all four CaV3.3 domains revealed preferential binding of Pn3a to the S3-S4 region of domain II (CaV3.3DII).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from chimeric channel studies.

claim: The S3-S4 region of CaV3.3 domain II represents a novel T-type channel pharmacological site.
source: This novel T-type channel pharmacological site was explored through computational docking simulations of Pn3a, site-directed mutagenesis, and full domain II swaps between CaV3 channels highlighting it as a subtype-specific pharmacophore.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental approaches including docking, mutagenesis, and domain swaps.

claim: Pn3a is suitable as a molecular tool in the study of the physiological roles of CaV3.3 channels.
source: This research expands our understanding of T-type calcium channel pharmacology and supports the suitability of Pn3a as a molecular tool in the study of the physiological roles of CaV3.3 channels.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing selective inhibition of CaV3.3.

claim: Voltage-gated calcium (CaV) channels are activated by membrane depolarization.
source: Voltage-gated calcium (CaV) channels are activated by membrane depolarization and are involved in many physiological processes including contraction, secretion, neurotransmitter release, and gene expression (Catterall et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about voltage-gated calcium channels, supported by citation.

claim: CaV channels are involved in many physiological processes including contraction, secretion, neurotransmitter release, and gene expression.
source: Voltage-gated calcium (CaV) channels are activated by membrane depolarization and are involved in many physiological processes including contraction, secretion, neurotransmitter release, and gene expression (Catterall et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Catterall et al., 2005.

claim: Low voltage-activated (LVA) currents mediated by T-type Ca2+ channels are activated by small membrane depolarization.
source: In contrast to high voltage-activated (HVA) Ca2+ currents mediated by L-, N-, P/Q-, and R-type calcium channels that require large depolarizations, low voltage-activated (LVA) currents mediated by T-type Ca2+ channels are activated by small membrane depolarization and display distinctively faster activation and inactivation kinetics.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the biophysical properties of T-type calcium channels.

claim: T-type Ca2+ channels display distinctively faster activation and inactivation kinetics compared to HVA channels.
source: In contrast to high voltage-activated (HVA) Ca2+ currents mediated by L-, N-, P/Q-, and R-type calcium channels that require large depolarizations, low voltage-activated (LVA) currents mediated by T-type Ca2+ channels are activated by small membrane depolarization and display distinctively faster activation and inactivation kinetics.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the kinetic properties of T-type channels.

claim: T-type channel activation near resting membrane potentials generates low-threshold Ca2+ spikes responsible for burst firing and low-frequency oscillatory discharges in thalamic, olivary, and cerebellar neurons.
source: T-type channel activation near resting membrane potentials generates low-threshold Ca2+ spikes responsible for the conspicuous burst firing and low-frequency oscillatory discharges observed in thalamic, olivary, and cerebellar neurons (Park et al., 2010; Dreyfus et al., 2010; Molineux et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The biophysical properties of T-type channels make them important regulators of cardiac and neuronal excitability.
source: Thus, the biophysical properties of the T-type channels make them important regulators of cardiac and neuronal excitability (Perez-Reyes, 2003; Huguenard, 1996; Coulter et al., 1989) and therefore key pharmacological targets for the treatment of neurological and psychiatric disorders (Zamponi, 2016; Maksemous et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: T-type channels are key pharmacological targets for the treatment of neurological and psychiatric disorders.
source: Thus, the biophysical properties of the T-type channels make them important regulators of cardiac and neuronal excitability (Perez-Reyes, 2003; Huguenard, 1996; Coulter et al., 1989) and therefore key pharmacological targets for the treatment of neurological and psychiatric disorders (Zamponi, 2016; Maksemous et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: T-type calcium channels display small single-channel conductance.
source: T-type calcium channels display small single-channel conductance (T stands for transient or tiny) (Perez-Reyes et al., 1998) and are encoded by the CACNA1G (CaV3.1), CACNA1H (CaV3.2), and CACNA1I (CaV3.3) genes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Perez-Reyes et al., 1998.

claim: T-type calcium channels are encoded by the CACNA1G (CaV3.1), CACNA1H (CaV3.2), and CACNA1I (CaV3.3) genes.
source: T-type calcium channels display small single-channel conductance (T stands for transient or tiny) (Perez-Reyes et al., 1998) and are encoded by the CACNA1G (CaV3.1), CACNA1H (CaV3.2), and CACNA1I (CaV3.3) genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the genetic encoding of T-type channels.

claim: CaV3 channels have similar channel activation and inactivation kinetics.
source: The CaV3s have similar channel activation and inactivation kinetics and are ubiquitously expressed in the nervous, neuroendocrine, reproductive, and cardiovascular systems (Perez-Reyes, 2003; Hansen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CaV3 channels are ubiquitously expressed in the nervous, neuroendocrine, reproductive, and cardiovascular systems.
source: The CaV3s have similar channel activation and inactivation kinetics and are ubiquitously expressed in the nervous, neuroendocrine, reproductive, and cardiovascular systems (Perez-Reyes, 2003; Hansen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CaV3.3-mediated currents display the slowest activation and inactivation kinetics in heterologous expression systems.
source: In heterologous expression systems, CaV3.3-mediated currents display the slowest activation and inactivation kinetics and recover faster from inactivation (Kozlov et al., 1999), however, due to these relatively small differences, they are nearly indistinguishable from the other T-type isoform in native tissue.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kozlov et al., 1999.

claim: CaV3.3 channels recover faster from inactivation compared to other T-type isoforms.
source: In heterologous expression systems, CaV3.3-mediated currents display the slowest activation and inactivation kinetics and recover faster from inactivation (Kozlov et al., 1999), however, due to these relatively small differences, they are nearly indistinguishable from the other T-type isoform in native tissue.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kozlov et al., 1999.

claim: CaV3.3 channels are nearly indistinguishable from other T-type isoforms in native tissue due to relatively small differences in kinetics.
source: In heterologous expression systems, CaV3.3-mediated currents display the slowest activation and inactivation kinetics and recover faster from inactivation (Kozlov et al., 1999), however, due to these relatively small differences, they are nearly indistinguishable from the other T-type isoform in native tissue.
evidence: This is an inference based on the small kinetic differences observed in heterologous systems.

claim: CACNA1I transcripts display remarkable regional distribution in the brain and appear to prevail in distal dendrites.
source: In the brain, abundant CACNA1I transcripts display remarkable regional distribution and appear to prevail in distal dendrites (Perez-Reyes, 2003; Lee et al., 1999), where CaV3.3 currents mediate the major sleep-spindle pacemaker in the thalamus (Astori et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CaV3.3 currents mediate the major sleep-spindle pacemaker in the thalamus.
source: In the brain, abundant CACNA1I transcripts display remarkable regional distribution and appear to prevail in distal dendrites (Perez-Reyes, 2003; Lee et al., 1999), where CaV3.3 currents mediate the major sleep-spindle pacemaker in the thalamus (Astori et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Astori et al., 2011.

claim: Transgenic mice lacking CaV3.3 channels display severe alterations to sleep-spindle generator rhythmogenic properties.
source: Transgenic mice lacking CaV3.3 channels display severe alterations to sleep-spindle generator rhythmogenic properties posing this T-type channel isoform as a critical target in the study of brain function and development (Astori et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Astori et al., 2011.

claim: CaV3.3 is a critical target in the study of brain function and development.
source: Transgenic mice lacking CaV3.3 channels display severe alterations to sleep-spindle generator rhythmogenic properties posing this T-type channel isoform as a critical target in the study of brain function and development (Astori et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the severe phenotype observed in knockout mice.

claim: The expression of CaV3.3 channels overlaps with that of CaV3.1 and/or CaV3.2.
source: However, the expression of CaV3.3 channels overlaps with that of CaV3.1 and/or CaV3.2, which together with the lack of robust, isoform-selective pharmacology has hampered the elucidation of their specific contributions to cellular physiology.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the expression patterns of T-type channels.

claim: The lack of robust, isoform-selective pharmacology has hampered the elucidation of specific contributions of CaV3.3 to cellular physiology.
source: However, the expression of CaV3.3 channels overlaps with that of CaV3.1 and/or CaV3.2, which together with the lack of robust, isoform-selective pharmacology has hampered the elucidation of their specific contributions to cellular physiology.
evidence: This is an inference about the challenges in studying CaV3.3 due to lack of selective tools.

claim: T-type calcium channels share the characteristic modular topology of other voltage-gated ion channels.
source: T-type calcium channels share the characteristic modular topology of other voltage-gated ion channels (VGICs) (Catterall et al., 2005) that consists of a voltage sensor (VS) module formed by transmembrane segments S1 through S4 and a pore module (PM) composed of the transmembrane segments S5 and S6 connected by a re-entrant pore loop.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Catterall et al., 2005.

claim: The voltage sensor module of VGICs is formed by transmembrane segments S1 through S4.
source: T-type calcium channels share the characteristic modular topology of other voltage-gated ion channels (VGICs) (Catterall et al., 2005) that consists of a voltage sensor (VS) module formed by transmembrane segments S1 through S4 and a pore module (PM) composed of the transmembrane segments S5 and S6 connected by a re-entrant pore loop.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VGIC structure.

claim: The pore module of VGICs is composed of transmembrane segments S5 and S6 connected by a re-entrant pore loop.
source: T-type calcium channels share the characteristic modular topology of other voltage-gated ion channels (VGICs) (Catterall et al., 2005) that consists of a voltage sensor (VS) module formed by transmembrane segments S1 through S4 and a pore module (PM) composed of the transmembrane segments S5 and S6 connected by a re-entrant pore loop.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VGIC structure.

claim: The voltage sensor controls channel opening in response to changes in membrane potential.
source: The VS controls channel opening in response to changes in membrane potential and the PM provides aqueous passage for ions across the lipid membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of the voltage sensor.

claim: The pore module provides aqueous passage for ions across the lipid membrane.
source: The VS controls channel opening in response to changes in membrane potential and the PM provides aqueous passage for ions across the lipid membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of the pore module.

claim: In voltage-gated potassium (KV) and transient receptor potential (TRP) channels, each monomer (1 × VS + 1 × PM) is encoded by a core α-subunit.
source: In voltage-gated potassium (KV) and transient receptor potential (TRP) channels, each monomer (1 × VS + 1 × PM) is encoded by a core α-subunit; whereas in voltage-gated sodium (NaV) and CaV channels, the α-subunit contains the four homologous, but not identical, domains (DI-DIV) joined through large intracellular linkers (Catterall, 2000; Catterall et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ion channel structure, supported by citations.

claim: In voltage-gated sodium (NaV) and CaV channels, the α-subunit contains four homologous, but not identical, domains (DI-DIV) joined through large intracellular linkers.
source: In voltage-gated potassium (KV) and transient receptor potential (TRP) channels, each monomer (1 × VS + 1 × PM) is encoded by a core α-subunit; whereas in voltage-gated sodium (NaV) and CaV channels, the α-subunit contains the four homologous, but not identical, domains (DI-DIV) joined through large intracellular linkers (Catterall, 2000; Catterall et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ion channel structure, supported by citations.

claim: Natural compounds that interact with ion channel voltage sensors are distinguished as gating modifiers.
source: Natural compounds that evolved to occlude ion channel's PM or to interact with their VS are distinguished broadly as pore blockers and gating modifiers, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the classification of ion channel modulators.

claim: At least three distinct pharmacological sites have been described in NaV channels.
source: In VGICs, the extracellularly exposed areas of the VS are pharmacological targets of neurotoxins and synthetic compounds where at least three distinct pharmacological sites have been described in NaV channels (Catterall et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Catterall et al., 2007.

claim: The S3b-S4 paddle motif within the voltage sensor is conserved and can be transplanted into the VS of other VGICs while retaining toxin sensitivity.
source: Within the VS is a conserved S3b-S4 paddle motif which can be transplanted into the VS of other VGICs and retain toxin sensitivity (Bosmans et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bosmans et al., 2008.

claim: α-Scorpion toxins, sea-anemone toxins, and numerous spider toxins interact with NaV channel site 3, located in the extracellular loop between DIV-S3 and DIV-S4.
source: α-Scorpion toxins, sea-anemone toxins, and numerous spider toxins interact with NaV channel site 3, located in the extracellular loop between DIV-S3 and DIV-S4 thereby interfering with the conformational changes that couple channel activation to fast inactivation (Hanck and Sheets, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hanck and Sheets, 2007.

claim: Toxins binding to NaV channel site 3 interfere with the conformational changes that couple channel activation to fast inactivation.
source: α-Scorpion toxins, sea-anemone toxins, and numerous spider toxins interact with NaV channel site 3, located in the extracellular loop between DIV-S3 and DIV-S4 thereby interfering with the conformational changes that couple channel activation to fast inactivation (Hanck and Sheets, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hanck and Sheets, 2007.

claim: β-scorpion toxins bind to the S1-S2 and S3-S4 loops of domain II (site 4) and shift the voltage dependence of channel activation towards depolarized voltages.
source: Binding of β-scorpion toxins to the S1-S2 and S3-S4 loops of domain II (site 4) shifts the voltage dependence of channel activation towards depolarized voltages reducing the maximal current at normal activation potentials.
evidence: This is established knowledge about β-scorpion toxin mechanism of action.

claim: Pharmacological site 6 in NaV channels is located near site 3 and is targeted by δ-conotoxins that slow NaV channel inactivation.
source: Lastly, pharmacological site 6 (located near site 3) is targeted by the δ-conotoxins that slow NaV channel inactivation (Terlau et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Terlau et al., 1996.

claim: Gating modifier peptides 'hold' the voltage sensor in different conformations leading to a mechanism recognized as 'VS trapping'.
source: All these gating modifier peptides (GMPs) appear to 'hold' the VS in different conformations leading to their mechanism of modulation to be recognized as 'VS trapping' (Cestèle et al., 1998), a phenomenon also observed in the interaction of theraphotoxins with KV2.1 (Swartz and MacKinnon, 1997) and agatoxins with CaV channels (McDonough et al., 1997a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sequence and functional conservation between voltage sensors leads to promiscuous interactions between peptides and small molecules across VGIC families.
source: Sequence and functional conservation between the VSs lead to promiscuous interactions between peptides and small molecules across VGIC families.
evidence: This is an inference based on observed cross-reactivity of toxins across channel families.

claim: ProTx-I interacts with NaV, KV, CaV, and TRPA1 channels.
source: Examples of these include ProTx-I (Thrixopelma pruriens, NaV/KV/CaV/TRPA1) (Bladen et al., 2014; Bosmans et al., 2008; Gui et al., 2014; Middleton et al., 2002); ProTx-II (T. pruriens, NaV/CaV) (Bladen et al., 2014; Middleton et al., 2002); Kurtoxin (Parabuthus transvaalicus, NaV/CaV) (Chuang et al., 1998); Hanatoxin (Grammostola spatulata, KV/NaV/CaV) (Bosmans et al., 2008; Li-Smerin and Swartz, 1998; Swartz and MacKinnon, 1997), and Pm1a (Pelinobius muticus, NaV/KV) (Finol-Urdaneta et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ProTx-II interacts with NaV and CaV channels.
source: Examples of these include ProTx-I (Thrixopelma pruriens, NaV/KV/CaV/TRPA1) (Bladen et al., 2014; Bosmans et al., 2008; Gui et al., 2014; Middleton et al., 2002); ProTx-II (T. pruriens, NaV/CaV) (Bladen et al., 2014; Middleton et al., 2002); Kurtoxin (Parabuthus transvaalicus, NaV/CaV) (Chuang et al., 1998); Hanatoxin (Grammostola spatulata, KV/NaV/CaV) (Bosmans et al., 2008; Li-Smerin and Swartz, 1998; Swartz and MacKinnon, 1997), and Pm1a (Pelinobius muticus, NaV/KV) (Finol-Urdaneta et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Kurtoxin interacts with NaV and CaV channels.
source: Examples of these include ProTx-I (Thrixopelma pruriens, NaV/KV/CaV/TRPA1) (Bladen et al., 2014; Bosmans et al., 2008; Gui et al., 2014; Middleton et al., 2002); ProTx-II (T. pruriens, NaV/CaV) (Bladen et al., 2014; Middleton et al., 2002); Kurtoxin (Parabuthus transvaalicus, NaV/CaV) (Chuang et al., 1998); Hanatoxin (Grammostola spatulata, KV/NaV/CaV) (Bosmans et al., 2008; Li-Smerin and Swartz, 1998; Swartz and MacKinnon, 1997), and Pm1a (Pelinobius muticus, NaV/KV) (Finol-Urdaneta et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chuang et al., 1998.

claim: Hanatoxin interacts with KV, NaV, and CaV channels.
source: Examples of these include ProTx-I (Thrixopelma pruriens, NaV/KV/CaV/TRPA1) (Bladen et al., 2014; Bosmans et al., 2008; Gui et al., 2014; Middleton et al., 2002); ProTx-II (T. pruriens, NaV/CaV) (Bladen et al., 2014; Middleton et al., 2002); Kurtoxin (Parabuthus transvaalicus, NaV/CaV) (Chuang et al., 1998); Hanatoxin (Grammostola spatulata, KV/NaV/CaV) (Bosmans et al., 2008; Li-Smerin and Swartz, 1998; Swartz and MacKinnon, 1997), and Pm1a (Pelinobius muticus, NaV/KV) (Finol-Urdaneta et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pm1a interacts with NaV and KV channels.
source: Examples of these include ProTx-I (Thrixopelma pruriens, NaV/KV/CaV/TRPA1) (Bladen et al., 2014; Bosmans et al., 2008; Gui et al., 2014; Middleton et al., 2002); ProTx-II (T. pruriens, NaV/CaV) (Bladen et al., 2014; Middleton et al., 2002); Kurtoxin (Parabuthus transvaalicus, NaV/CaV) (Chuang et al., 1998); Hanatoxin (Grammostola spatulata, KV/NaV/CaV) (Bosmans et al., 2008; Li-Smerin and Swartz, 1998; Swartz and MacKinnon, 1997), and Pm1a (Pelinobius muticus, NaV/KV) (Finol-Urdaneta et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Finol-Urdaneta et al., 2022.

claim: Small molecules such as capsaicin, capsazepine, and A803467 interact across VGIC families.
source: Furthermore, small molecules such as capsaicin, capsazepine (TRPV1/KV/CaV) (Caterina et al., 1997; Kuenzi and Dale, 1996; McArthur et al., 2019), and A803467 (NaV, CaV) (Bladen and Zamponi, 2012) amongst others are known to interact across VGIC families.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Shared ancestry and sequence conservation within the voltage sensing machinery rationalize commonalities in structure, gating kinetics, and pharmacophores between NaV and T-type channels.
source: Shared ancestry and sequence conservation within the voltage sensing machinery have been used to rationalize commonalities in structure, gating kinetics, and pharmacophores between NaV and T-type channels (Bladen and Zamponi, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bladen and Zamponi, 2012.

claim: Several NaV-active GMPs inhibit CaV3.1 channels through interactions with the channel's domain III (CaV3.1DIII).
source: Several NaV-active GMPs were shown to inhibit CaV3.1 channels through interactions with the channel's domain III (CaV3.1DIII) (Salari et al., 2016); whereas the potent NaV1.7 inhibitor, µ-theraphotoxin Pn3a (Pamphobeteus nigricolour) (Deuis et al., 2017), also interacts with HVA CaV channels (McArthur et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Salari et al., 2016.

claim: µ-theraphotoxin Pn3a is a potent NaV1.7 inhibitor.
source: Several NaV-active GMPs were shown to inhibit CaV3.1 channels through interactions with the channel's domain III (CaV3.1DIII) (Salari et al., 2016); whereas the potent NaV1.7 inhibitor, µ-theraphotoxin Pn3a (Pamphobeteus nigricolour) (Deuis et al., 2017), also interacts with HVA CaV channels (McArthur et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deuis et al., 2017.

claim: Pn3a interacts with HVA CaV channels.
source: Several NaV-active GMPs were shown to inhibit CaV3.1 channels through interactions with the channel's domain III (CaV3.1DIII) (Salari et al., 2016); whereas the potent NaV1.7 inhibitor, µ-theraphotoxin Pn3a (Pamphobeteus nigricolour) (Deuis et al., 2017), also interacts with HVA CaV channels (McArthur et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McArthur et al., 2020.

claim: Pn3a (10 µM) strongly inhibited CaV3.3-mediated currents (90.2% ± 1.9%, n=5).
source: Pn3a (10 µM) strongly inhibited CaV3.3-mediated currents (90.2% ± 1.9%, n=5) with negligible effects over the two other T-type isoforms (CaV3.1: 3.8% ± 1.8%, n=5; CaV3.2: 2.5% ± 2.5%, n=5) (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Pn3a (10 µM) has negligible effects on CaV3.1 (3.8% ± 1.8%, n=5) and CaV3.2 (2.5% ± 2.5%, n=5).
source: Pn3a (10 µM) strongly inhibited CaV3.3-mediated currents (90.2% ± 1.9%, n=5) with negligible effects over the two other T-type isoforms (CaV3.1: 3.8% ± 1.8%, n=5; CaV3.2: 2.5% ± 2.5%, n=5) (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Scaled CaV3.3 macroscopic currents recorded in the absence and presence of Pn3a (3 µM) display similar macroscopic activation kinetics.
source: Scaled CaV3.3 macroscopic currents recorded in the absence (control) and presence of Pn3a (3 µM) display similar macroscopic activation kinetics (τact, control = 5.95 ± 0.54 ms vs. τact, Pn3a = 6.37 ± 0.44 ms; p=0.32, n=5, paired t-test), whereas Pn3a slowed macroscopic inactivation kinetics (τinact control = 39.91 ± 8.25 ms vs. τinact, Pn3a = 60.25 ± 16.02 ms; p=0.04, n=5, paired t-test) (representative currents provided in the inset, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Pn3a slowed CaV3.3 macroscopic inactivation kinetics (τinact control = 39.91 ± 8.25 ms vs. τinact, Pn3a = 60.25 ± 16.02 ms; p=0.04, n=5).
source: Scaled CaV3.3 macroscopic currents recorded in the absence (control) and presence of Pn3a (3 µM) display similar macroscopic activation kinetics (τact, control = 5.95 ± 0.54 ms vs. τact, Pn3a = 6.37 ± 0.44 ms; p=0.32, n=5, paired t-test), whereas Pn3a slowed macroscopic inactivation kinetics (τinact control = 39.91 ± 8.25 ms vs. τinact, Pn3a = 60.25 ± 16.02 ms; p=0.04, n=5, paired t-test) (representative currents provided in the inset, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Pn3a inhibits CaV3.3 currents with an IC50 value of 0.96±0.05 µM.
source: Fit to a standard Hill equation rendered an IC50 value of 0.96±0.05 µM (nH 0.87±0.04, n=5 per concentration) for the inhibition of CaV3.3 channels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from concentration-response curves.

claim: The Hill coefficient for Pn3a inhibition of CaV3.3 is 0.87±0.04, consistent with a 1:1 stoichiometry between Pn3a toxin and CaV3.3 channels.
source: This Hill coefficient is consistent with a 1:1 stoichiometry between Pn3a toxin and CaV3.3 channels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Hill coefficient value obtained from experimental data.

claim: The on-rate constant (kon) for Pn3a binding to CaV3.3 is 0.036 µM–1 s–1.
source: The linear regression line results in a kon of 0.036 µM–1 s–1 and koff of 0.052 s–1 which yield a KD of 1.4 µM, in close agreement with the IC50 value obtained (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from kinetic analysis.

claim: The off-rate constant (koff) for Pn3a binding to CaV3.3 is 0.052 s–1.
source: The linear regression line results in a kon of 0.036 µM–1 s–1 and koff of 0.052 s–1 which yield a KD of 1.4 µM, in close agreement with the IC50 value obtained (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from kinetic analysis.

claim: The KD for Pn3a binding to CaV3.3 is 1.4 µM.
source: The linear regression line results in a kon of 0.036 µM–1 s–1 and koff of 0.052 s–1 which yield a KD of 1.4 µM, in close agreement with the IC50 value obtained (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental kinetic data.

claim: CaV3.3 activation is shifted ~13 mV to more depolarized potentials in the presence of Pn3a (3 µM).
source: CaV3.3 activation is shifted ~13 mV to more depolarized potentials (control V0.5 = −28.3±0.4 mV, n=5, vs. Pn3a V0.5 = −15.3±0.4 mV, n=5; p<0.0001), indicating that a stronger depolarization is required to enable channel opening in the presence of Pn3a (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from voltage-dependence studies.

claim: The voltage dependence of CaV3.3 steady-state inactivation (SSI) was not affected by exposure to Pn3a.
source: The voltage dependence of CaV3.3 steady-state inactivation (SSI) was not affected by exposure to the spider peptide (control V0.5 = −56.3±0.3 mV, n=5, vs. Pn3a V0.5 = −56.6±0.4 mV, n=5, p=0.57, Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: CaV3.3-mediated currents recovered faster from inactivation in the presence of Pn3a (τ=0.22 ± 0.01 s, n=5) than under control conditions (τ=0.34 ± 0.01 s, n=5; p<0.0001).
source: Consistent with the observed slowing of inactivation, CaV3.3-mediated currents inactivated by a 200 ms pre-pulse to –20 mV recovered faster in the presence of Pn3a (τ=0.22 ± 0.01 s, n=5) than under control conditions (τ=0.34 ± 0.01 s, n=5; p<0.0001) (Figure 2D–E), suggesting a potential Pn3a-dependent destabilization of the inactivated state.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Pn3a may destabilize the inactivated state of CaV3.3.
source: Consistent with the observed slowing of inactivation, CaV3.3-mediated currents inactivated by a 200 ms pre-pulse to –20 mV recovered faster in the presence of Pn3a (τ=0.22 ± 0.01 s, n=5) than under control conditions (τ=0.34 ± 0.01 s, n=5; p<0.0001) (Figure 2D–E), suggesting a potential Pn3a-dependent destabilization of the inactivated state.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed faster recovery from inactivation.

claim: Pn3a displayed a decrease in CaV3.3 ICa inhibition at more depolarized potentials.
source: Pn3A displayed a decrease in CaV3.3 ICa inhibition at more depolarized potentials consistent with Pn3a preferentially binding to the down-state of the VS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from voltage-dependence studies.

claim: Pn3a preferentially binds to the down-state of the voltage sensor.
source: Pn3A displayed a decrease in CaV3.3 ICa inhibition at more depolarized potentials consistent with Pn3a preferentially binding to the down-state of the VS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the voltage-dependent inhibition pattern.

claim: Pn3a-modified CaV3.3 currents displayed a faster deactivation time constant (τdeactivation) across all potentials tested compared to control.
source: Pn3a-modified CaV3.3 currents displayed a faster deactivation time constant (τdeactivation) across all potentials tested compared to control (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from tail current analysis.

claim: Pn3a binding may destabilize the open state or stabilize the closed state of CaV3.3.
source: This data suggests that Pn3a binding may destabilize the open state or stabilize the closed one.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed faster deactivation kinetics.

claim: Pn3a is a CaV3.3 gating modifier peptide that decreases channel availability by increasing the energy required for channel opening.
source: This results that Pn3a is a CaV3.3 GMP that decreases channel availability by increasing the energy required for channel opening.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed depolarizing shift in activation.

claim: All four KV1.7/CaV3.3 chimeric constructs were functional, mediating large K+ currents.
source: All four KV1.7/CaV3.3 chimeric constructs were functional, mediating large K+ currents that displayed distinct gating properties from those of the parental wild-type KV1.7 (V0.5 = −10.5±0.6 mV, n=7; Figure 4B, inset).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from chimeric channel studies.

claim: Chimeric KV1.7/CaV3.3DI, KV1.7/CaV3.3DII and KV1.7/CaV3.3DIII displayed 80–100 mV depolarizing shifts in channel activation.
source: Briefly, chimeric KV1.7/CaV3.3DI, KV1.7/CaV3.3DII and KV1.7/CaV3.3DIII displayed 80–100 mV depolarizing shifts in channel activation (KV1.7/CaV3.3DI V0.5=91.3 ± 0.4 mV, n=5; KV1.7/CaV3.3DII V0.5=97.3 ± 0.4 mV, n=9; KV1.7/CaV3.3DIII V0.5=71.3 ± 0.8 mV, n=7, two-way ANOVA, p<0.05), whereas KV1.7/CaV3.3DIV activation was ~50 mV hyperpolarized (KV1.7/CaV3.3DIV V0.5 = −60.8±0.8 mV, n=5; two-way ANOVA, p<0.05) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: KV1.7/CaV3.3DIV activation was ~50 mV hyperpolarized compared to wild-type KV1.7.
source: Briefly, chimeric KV1.7/CaV3.3DI, KV1.7/CaV3.3DII and KV1.7/CaV3.3DIII displayed 80–100 mV depolarizing shifts in channel activation (KV1.7/CaV3.3DI V0.5=91.3 ± 0.4 mV, n=5; KV1.7/CaV3.3DII V0.5=97.3 ± 0.4 mV, n=9; KV1.7/CaV3.3DIII V0.5=71.3 ± 0.8 mV, n=7, two-way ANOVA, p<0.05), whereas KV1.7/CaV3.3DIV activation was ~50 mV hyperpolarized (KV1.7/CaV3.3DIV V0.5 = −60.8±0.8 mV, n=5; two-way ANOVA, p<0.05) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Peak currents of KV1.7/CaV3.3DI and KV1.7/CaV3.3DIV chimeras were insensitive to Pn3a.
source: Similar to the parental channel, peak currents of KV1.7/CaV3.3DI and KV1.7/CaV3.3DIV chimaeras were insensitive to Pn3a (KV1.7: 1.0% ± 0.8%, n=6; CaV3.3DI: 0.6% ± 0.5%, n=5, and CaV3.3DIV: 0.4% ± 0.2%, n=5) (Figure 5A, D and E), with KV1.7/CaV3.3DIII displaying modest peptide-dependent inhibition (12.0% ± 0.6%, n=6) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from chimeric channel studies.

claim: KV1.7/CaV3.3DIII displayed modest peptide-dependent inhibition by Pn3a (12.0% ± 0.6%, n=6).
source: Similar to the parental channel, peak currents of KV1.7/CaV3.3DI and KV1.7/CaV3.3DIV chimaeras were insensitive to Pn3a (KV1.7: 1.0% ± 0.8%, n=6; CaV3.3DI: 0.6% ± 0.5%, n=5, and CaV3.3DIV: 0.4% ± 0.2%, n=5) (Figure 5A, D and E), with KV1.7/CaV3.3DIII displaying modest peptide-dependent inhibition (12.0% ± 0.6%, n=6) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from chimeric channel studies.

claim: Currents mediated by KV1.7/CaV3.3DII were significantly reduced (54.2% ± 2.9%, n=7) in the presence of Pn3a.
source: In contrast, currents mediated by KV1.7/CaV3.3DII were significantly reduced (54.2% ± 2.9%, n=7) in the presence of Pn3a (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from chimeric channel studies.

claim: Pn3a induced an ~15 mV rightward shift in the half voltage of activation (V0.5) exclusively in the CaV3.3DII chimera.
source: The latter analysis revealed an ~15 mV rightward shift in the half voltage of activation (V0.5) exclusively in the CaV3.3DII chimera when exposed to Pn3a (control V0.5=97.3 ± 0.4 mV, n=9; vs. Pn3a V0.5=112.6 ± 0.4 mV, n=7, p<0.0001), strongly suggesting that Pn3a interacts with the S3-S4 region of domain II in CaV3.3.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Replacement of CaV3.3DII with CaV3.1DII resulted in partial loss of Pn3a inhibition (CaV3.3/CaV3.1DII: 33% ± 4.1%, n=5).
source: Replacement of CaV3.3DII with either CaV3.1DII or CaV3.2DII resulted in partial (CaV3.3/CaV3.1DII: 33% ± 4.1%, n=5, one-way ANOVA p<0.0001) or complete (CaV3.3/CaV3.2DII: 2.2% ± 1.5%, n=5, one-way ANOVA p<0.0001) loss of inhibition compared to the full-length CaV3.3 (90.2 ± 1.9% n=5) in the presence of 10 μM Pn3a (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Replacement of CaV3.3DII with CaV3.2DII resulted in complete loss of Pn3a inhibition (CaV3.3/CaV3.2DII: 2.2% ± 1.5%, n=5).
source: Replacement of CaV3.3DII with either CaV3.1DII or CaV3.2DII resulted in partial (CaV3.3/CaV3.1DII: 33% ± 4.1%, n=5, one-way ANOVA p<0.0001) or complete (CaV3.3/CaV3.2DII: 2.2% ± 1.5%, n=5, one-way ANOVA p<0.0001) loss of inhibition compared to the full-length CaV3.3 (90.2 ± 1.9% n=5) in the presence of 10 μM Pn3a (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: CaV3.1/CaV3.3DII currents were inhibited by 71.4% ± 4.1% (n=5) by Pn3a.
source: The reverse constructs where CaV3.3DII was grafted onto CaV3.1 (CaV3.1/CaV3.3DII) or CaV3.2 (CaV3.2/CaV3.3DII) afforded Pn3a sensitivity to the parental CaV3 channel such that currents mediated by CaV3.1/CaV3.3DII were inhibited by 71.4% ± 4.1% (n=5), and CaV3.2/CaV3.3DII by 68.0% ± 3.6% (n=5) (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from domain swap studies.

claim: CaV3.2/CaV3.3DII currents were inhibited by 68.0% ± 3.6% (n=5) by Pn3a.
source: The reverse constructs where CaV3.3DII was grafted onto CaV3.1 (CaV3.1/CaV3.3DII) or CaV3.2 (CaV3.2/CaV3.3DII) afforded Pn3a sensitivity to the parental CaV3 channel such that currents mediated by CaV3.1/CaV3.3DII were inhibited by 71.4% ± 4.1% (n=5), and CaV3.2/CaV3.3DII by 68.0% ± 3.6% (n=5) (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from domain swap studies.

claim: CaV3.3DII is required for Pn3a interaction with T-type calcium channels.
source: Thus, verifying that CaV3.3DII is required for Pn3a interaction with T-type calcium channels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the domain swap experimental results.

claim: Pn3a forms fewer contacts with the DII S3-S4 linker of CaV3.1 and CaV3.2, compared to CaV3.3.
source: Comparative analyses of toxin interactions with the other T-type calcium channel members showed that Pn3a forms fewer contacts with the DII S3-S4 linker of CaV3.1 and CaV3.2, compared to CaV3.3 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by computational docking simulations.

claim: Pn3a-K17 is predicted to be in close proximity to CaV3.3-D689 and may form a salt bridge contact.
source: In particular, Pn3a-K17 is predicted to be in close proximity to D689 and may form an especially strong interaction due to the possibility of a salt bridge contact.
evidence: This is based on computational docking predictions.

claim: CaV3.3-D689A displayed significant reduction in Pn3a inhibition (27.6% ± 1.8%, n=5).
source: In comparison to wild-type CaV3.3, CaV3.3-D689A (27.6% ± 1.8%, n=5, one-way ANOVA p<0.0001) and CaV3.3-E628A (68.2% ± 2.0%, n=5, one-way ANOVA p<0.0001) displayed significant reductions in Pn3a inhibition (Figure 6F), whereas the peptide activity in the other mutants studied (CaV3.3-Q687A: 83.6% ± 0.5%, n=5; CaV3.3-R696A: 83.6% ± 2.7%, n=5; CaV3.3-K1294A: 84.8% ± 1.2%, n=5; CaV3.3-N1310A 79.2% ± 3.5%, n=5; and CaV3.3-Q1362A 85.4% ± 1.3%, n=5) was unaffected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies with statistical analysis.

claim: CaV3.3-E628A displayed significant reduction in Pn3a inhibition (68.2% ± 2.0%, n=5).
source: In comparison to wild-type CaV3.3, CaV3.3-D689A (27.6% ± 1.8%, n=5, one-way ANOVA p<0.0001) and CaV3.3-E628A (68.2% ± 2.0%, n=5, one-way ANOVA p<0.0001) displayed significant reductions in Pn3a inhibition (Figure 6F), whereas the peptide activity in the other mutants studied (CaV3.3-Q687A: 83.6% ± 0.5%, n=5; CaV3.3-R696A: 83.6% ± 2.7%, n=5; CaV3.3-K1294A: 84.8% ± 1.2%, n=5; CaV3.3-N1310A 79.2% ± 3.5%, n=5; and CaV3.3-Q1362A 85.4% ± 1.3%, n=5) was unaffected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies with statistical analysis.

claim: Pn3a activity in CaV3.3-Q687A, CaV3.3-R696A, CaV3.3-K1294A, CaV3.3-N1310A, and CaV3.3-Q1362A mutants was unaffected.
source: In comparison to wild-type CaV3.3, CaV3.3-D689A (27.6% ± 1.8%, n=5, one-way ANOVA p<0.0001) and CaV3.3-E628A (68.2% ± 2.0%, n=5, one-way ANOVA p<0.0001) displayed significant reductions in Pn3a inhibition (Figure 6F), whereas the peptide activity in the other mutants studied (CaV3.3-Q687A: 83.6% ± 0.5%, n=5; CaV3.3-R696A: 83.6% ± 2.7%, n=5; CaV3.3-K1294A: 84.8% ± 1.2%, n=5; CaV3.3-N1310A 79.2% ± 3.5%, n=5; and CaV3.3-Q1362A 85.4% ± 1.3%, n=5) was unaffected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies.

claim: Pn3a is a gating modifier inhibitor of human CaV3.3 channels with >100-fold higher activity over CaV3.1 and CaV3.2.
source: The present study demonstrates the functional activity of Pn3a as a gating modifier inhibitor of human CaV3.3 channels with >100-fold higher activity over CaV3.1 and CaV3.2.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Pn3a is the first molecular probe available for the study of CaV3.3 contribution in native cells.
source: Thus, this investigation highlights Pn3a as the first molecular probe available for the study of CaV3.3 contribution in native cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the selectivity data presented.

claim: The unique features of Pn3a's CaV3.3 specificity may be exploited to design isoform-selective T-type calcium channel modulators.
source: We propose that the unique features of Pn3a's CaV3.3 specificity may be exploited to design isoform-selective T-type calcium channel modulators.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications based on the findings.

claim: µ-Theraphotoxin Pn3a was originally described as a potent NaV1.7 inhibitor with an IC50 of 0.9 nM.
source: µ-Theraphotoxin Pn3a was originally described as a potent NaV1.7 inhibitor with an IC50 of 0.9 nM, while also inhibiting other tetrodotoxin-sensitive NaV channels (NaV1.1–1.4 and NaV1.6) with 10- to 100-fold less potency (Deuis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deuis et al., 2017.

claim: Pn3a inhibits tetrodotoxin-sensitive NaV channels (NaV1.1–1.4 and NaV1.6) with 10- to 100-fold less potency than NaV1.7.
source: µ-Theraphotoxin Pn3a was originally described as a potent NaV1.7 inhibitor with an IC50 of 0.9 nM, while also inhibiting other tetrodotoxin-sensitive NaV channels (NaV1.1–1.4 and NaV1.6) with 10- to 100-fold less potency (Deuis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deuis et al., 2017.

claim: Pn3a inhibits murine dorsal root ganglion HVA ICa and human CaV1.2, CaV1.3, CaV2.1, and CaV2.2 calcium channels expressed in HEK293T cells (IC50 3–10 μM).
source: More recently Pn3a was shown to inhibit murine dorsal root ganglion HVA ICa and human CaV1.2, CaV1.3, CaV2.1, and CaV2.2 calcium channels expressed in HEK293T cells (IC50 3–10 μM) (McArthur et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McArthur et al., 2020.

claim: Kurtoxin was the first gating modifier peptide reported to modulate CaV3 channels with a high affinity for CaV3.1 and CaV3.2 channels.
source: The scorpion peptide Kurtoxin was the first GMP reported to modulate CaV3 channels with a high affinity for CaV3.1 and CaV3.2 channels (Chuang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chuang et al., 1998.

claim: KLI inhibits CaV3.3 with an IC50 ~ 450 nM.
source: The closely related peptide KLI, from Parabuthus granulatus, was later shown to inhibit CaV3.3 with an IC50 ~ 450 nM (Olamendi-Portugal et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Olamendi-Portugal et al., 2002.

claim: ProTx-I preferentially modulates CaV3.1 channels.
source: The activity of spider Protoxins I and II against the three CaV3 channels revealed that ProTx-I preferentially modulates CaV3.1 channels, whereas ProTx-II targets CaV3.2 (Bladen et al., 2014; Salari et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bladen et al., 2014 and Salari et al., 2016.

claim: ProTx-II targets CaV3.2 channels.
source: The activity of spider Protoxins I and II against the three CaV3 channels revealed that ProTx-I preferentially modulates CaV3.1 channels, whereas ProTx-II targets CaV3.2 (Bladen et al., 2014; Salari et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bladen et al., 2014 and Salari et al., 2016.

claim: Pn3a complements the molecular toolbox for the study of T-type calcium channels in native tissues.
source: Thus, Pn3a complements the molecular toolbox for the study of T-type calcium channels in native tissues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the selectivity profile of Pn3a compared to other available tools.

claim: Pn3a inhibits CaV3.3 by inducing a depolarizing shift in CaV3.3 voltage dependence of activation in a manner analogous to Kurtoxin, Protoxin I, and Protoxin II actions on CaV3.1 channels.
source: Pn3a inhibits CaV3.3 by inducing a depolarizing shift in CaV3.3 voltage dependence of activation in a manner analogous to Kurtoxin, Protoxin I, and Protoxin II actions on CaV3.1 channels (Edgerton et al., 2010; Chuang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and comparison with experimental data.

claim: Pn3a's modulation of CaV3.3 is consistent with Pn3a's modulation of NaV1.7.
source: This is also consistent with Pn3a's modulation of NaV1.7 (Deuis et al., 2017) but not of CaV2.2 channels for which a hyperpolarizing shift in the voltage dependence of inactivation was associated with current inhibition (McArthur et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pn3a induces a hyperpolarizing shift in the voltage dependence of inactivation of CaV2.2 channels.
source: This is also consistent with Pn3a's modulation of NaV1.7 (Deuis et al., 2017) but not of CaV2.2 channels for which a hyperpolarizing shift in the voltage dependence of inactivation was associated with current inhibition (McArthur et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McArthur et al., 2020.

claim: Pn3a causes twofold slower recovery from inactivation in NaV1.7 channels.
source: In contrast to the twofold slower recovery from inactivation reported for Pn3a-bound NaV1.7 channels, currents mediated by Pn3a-modified CaV3.3 channels recover ~1.5-fold faster from inactivation (Figure 2D/E).
evidence: This is an implicit reference to previous findings about Pn3a effects on NaV1.7.

claim: Voltage-dependent unbinding of toxin at more positive potentials could contribute to an apparent faster recovery from inactivation as reported for CaV active toxins such as AgaIVA and SNX482.
source: Nevertheless, given Pn3a's voltage dependence of Cav3.3 inhibition (Figure 3A), voltage-dependent unbinding of the toxin at more positive potentials could also contribute to an apparent faster recovery from inactivation as reported for CaV active toxins such as AgaIVA (McDonough et al., 1997b) and SNX482 (Bourinet et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous studies on other toxins.

claim: Pn3a inhibition of CaV3.3 was voltage-dependent with greater inhibition at more negative potentials similar to Kurtoxin-inhibited CaV3.1 channel currents.
source: Pn3a inhibition of CaV3.3 was voltage-dependent with greater inhibition at more negative potentials (Figure 3A) similar to Kurtoxin-inhibited CaV3.1 channel currents (Chuang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to Chuang et al., 1998.

claim: A delay in CaV3.1 activation kinetics was apparent in the presence of both Kurtoxin and ProTx-II but not in Pn3a-modified CaV3.3.
source: However, a delay in CaV3.1 activation kinetics was apparent in the presence of both Kurtoxin and ProTx-II (Edgerton et al., 2010; Chuang et al., 1998) but not in Pn3a-modified CaV3.3.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and comparison with experimental data.

claim: Pn3a and ProTx-II appear to slow T-type channel deactivation suggestive of stabilization of the channel's closed state.
source: The spider peptides Pn3a (this study) and ProTx-II (Edgerton et al., 2010) appear to slow T-type channel deactivation suggestive of stabilization of the channel's closed state, whereas Kurtoxin, from scorpion venom, does not affect CaV3.1 channel closure (Chuang et al., 1998) highlighting incompletely understood aspects of GMP/VGIC interactions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Kurtoxin does not affect CaV3.1 channel closure.
source: The spider peptides Pn3a (this study) and ProTx-II (Edgerton et al., 2010) appear to slow T-type channel deactivation suggestive of stabilization of the channel's closed state, whereas Kurtoxin, from scorpion venom, does not affect CaV3.1 channel closure (Chuang et al., 1998) highlighting incompletely understood aspects of GMP/VGIC interactions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chuang et al., 1998.

claim: The portability of the S3-S4 paddle region was shown more than 20 years ago.
source: The portability of the S3-S4 paddle region was shown more than 20 years ago (Swartz and MacKinnon, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Swartz and MacKinnon, 1997.

claim: Most studies have used the KV2.1 channel backbone for the identification of GMPs binding sites in NaV and CaV channels expressed in Xenopus oocytes.
source: To date, most studies, if not all, have used the KV2.1 channel backbone for the identification of GMPs binding sites in NaV and CaV channels expressed in Xenopus oocytes (Bosmans et al., 2008; Salari et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: KV1.7 was selected as the chimera backbone given the remarkable scarcity of GMPs interacting with KV1 channels.
source: For our chimera studies, we selected the KV1.7 backbone given the remarkable scarcity of GMPs interacting with KV1 channels (Finol-Urdaneta et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Finol-Urdaneta et al., 2020.

claim: KV1.7 exhibits robust expression in heterologous systems.
source: The robust expression of this channel in heterologous systems (Finol-Urdaneta et al., 2006; Finol-Urdaneta et al., 2012) and resistance to Pn3a modulation (Figure 5E/F) make it suitable to assess peptide binding to CaV3.3 paddle motifs in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: KV1.7 is resistant to Pn3a modulation.
source: The robust expression of this channel in heterologous systems (Finol-Urdaneta et al., 2006; Finol-Urdaneta et al., 2012) and resistance to Pn3a modulation (Figure 5E/F) make it suitable to assess peptide binding to CaV3.3 paddle motifs in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: ProTx-II, PaTx-1, GsAF-I, and GsAF-II exert their inhibitory actions predominantly through interaction with CaV3.1DIII.
source: Analogous chimeric approaches of KV2.1/CaV3.1DI-IV have indicated that ProTx-II, PaTx-1, GsAF-I, and GsAF-II exert their inhibitory actions predominantly through interaction with CaV3.1DIII (Salari et al., 2016), whereas Pn3a does so by targeting KV2.1/NaV1.7DII and KV2.1/NaV1.7DIV (Deuis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Salari et al., 2016.

claim: Pn3a targets KV2.1/NaV1.7DII and KV2.1/NaV1.7DIV.
source: Analogous chimeric approaches of KV2.1/CaV3.1DI-IV have indicated that ProTx-II, PaTx-1, GsAF-I, and GsAF-II exert their inhibitory actions predominantly through interaction with CaV3.1DIII (Salari et al., 2016), whereas Pn3a does so by targeting KV2.1/NaV1.7DII and KV2.1/NaV1.7DIV (Deuis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deuis et al., 2017.

claim: DI-DIII are important for NaV activation.
source: A substantial body of literature has shown that DI-DIII and DIV are important for NaV activation and inactivation, respectively (Ahern et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ahern et al., 2016.

claim: DIV is important for NaV inactivation.
source: A substantial body of literature has shown that DI-DIII and DIV are important for NaV activation and inactivation, respectively (Ahern et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ahern et al., 2016.

claim: The predominant effects of Pn3a on CaV3.3 activation are consistent with its interaction with DII of this channel.
source: Thus, the predominant effects of Pn3a on CaV3.3 activation are consistent with its interaction with DII of this channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known roles of different domains in channel function.

claim: ProTx-I inhibits CaV3.3/CaV3.1DIV chimeric channels while interacting less potently with CaV3.3/CaV3.1DII.
source: Furthermore, it has been shown that ProTx-I inhibits CaV3.3/CaV3.1DIV chimeric channels while interacting less potently with CaV3.3/CaV3.1DII.
evidence: This is a reference to previous findings about ProTx-I.

claim: A clear binding site for ProTx-I could not be delineated through mutation of individual CaV3.1DII residues.
source: However, a clear binding site could not be delineated through mutation of individual CaV3.1DII residues as those did not result in measurable changes in toxin affinity (Bladen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bladen et al., 2014.

claim: Aspartate in position 689 of CaV3.3DII constitutes an important interaction site for Pn3a.
source: Our domain swap experiments verified that Pn3a's actions are largely determined by CaV3.3DII from which aspartate in position 689 constitutes an important interaction site as shown by its alanine replacement in CaV3.3 and KV1.7/CaV3.3DII.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies.

claim: Subtle, but significant GMP/VGIC interaction differences highlight incompletely understood idiosyncrasies related to molecular aspects of ion channel function between isoforms.
source: It can be surmised that subtle, but significant GMP/VGIC interaction differences highlight incompletely understood idiosyncrasies related to molecular aspects of ion channel function between isoforms as well as how peptide interactions may be affected by the experimental manipulation and conditions used for their study.
evidence: This is a speculation about the complexity of toxin-channel interactions.

claim: Pn3a binds within the groove formed between extracellular linkers S1-S2 and S3-S4 supported by electrostatic interactions with the CaV3.3DII S3-S4 paddle.
source: Our molecular docking calculations suggest that Pn3a binds within the groove formed between extracellular linkers S1-S2 and S3-S4 supported by electrostatic interactions with the CaV3.3DII S3-S4 paddle, which bears some similarity with the CaV3.1/ProTx-II complex in which favourable binding sites occur in CaV3.1's DII and DIV (Bladen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by computational docking simulations and citation to previous work.

claim: The interaction of Pn3a with CaV3.3 channels involves substantial interactions within the S3-S4 paddle (K17-Q687) and S4 (H18-R696) of CaV3.3DII.
source: The interaction of Pn3a with CaV3.3 channels involves substantial interactions within the S3-S4 paddle (K17-Q687) and S4 (H18-R696) of CaV3.3DII, while a close contact may also exist between the sidechain of D689 and the sidechain of Pn3a-K17 (Figure 6D, upper left panel).
evidence: This is supported by computational docking simulations.

claim: The predicted Pn3a interaction with CaV3.3 appears to share overall similarities with previously identified spider peptide toxins modulating NaV and KV channels.
source: Hence, the predicted Pn3a interaction with CaV3.3 appears to share overall similarities with previously identified spider peptide toxins modulating NaV and KV channels in which the common bioactive surface consists of positively charged and hydrophobic residues (Smith et al., 2007; Corzo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pn3a interacts with the paddle motif of DII's voltage sensor module through putative stabilization of the closed/resting state and concomitant channel current inhibition.
source: The findings presented here establish Pn3a as a gating modifier modulator of CaV3.3 channels interacting with the paddle motif of DII's VS module through putative stabilization of the closed/resting state and concomitant channel current inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Pn3a's>100-fold higher potency against CaV3.3 over the other two CaV3 isoforms is rationalized through recognition of a previously unknown drug binding site.
source: Pn3a's>100-fold higher potency against CaV3.3 over the other two CaV3 isoforms is rationalized through recognition of a previously unknown drug binding site that may be exploited in the design of isoform-selective CaV3 channel modulators.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental and computational findings.

claim: The novel binding site identified for Pn3a may be exploited in the design of isoform-selective CaV3 channel modulators.
source: Pn3a's>100-fold higher potency against CaV3.3 over the other two CaV3 isoforms is rationalized through recognition of a previously unknown drug binding site that may be exploited in the design of isoform-selective CaV3 channel modulators.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications of the findings.
